scenario: AITA for telling an intern to throw her banana peel in the trash? | A few details to set the stage: To get into my place of work, one needs to walk from the parking lot down a sidewalk that is along the side of the building. The other side of the sidewalk is semi-wooded with low growing evergreen shrubs. This sidewalk is about 100ft long, and has a trash can at either end. Also, in the last month, there have been a ton of flies buzzing around this area, so much so that the building manager called an exterminator. This morning, I (\~30s F) witnessed an intern (20s F) for one of the companies in our building walking into work eating a banana. About 3/4 of the way down the sidewalk, with a trashcan not even 25 feet away, she tossed the banana peel into the bushes. It landed on top of the bush and she just kept walking. I wasn't sufficiently caffeinated to be polite, so I blurted out "What the hell? There's a trash can right in front of you!" complete with the WTF hand gesture; pointing to the trash can. She ripped into me, claiming it's organic and feeds the animals. She was half yelling / half crying. I pointed at the peel sitting on top of the bush and told her to "pick up your (her) damn banana peel." Instead she cried loudly saying something unintelligible, got her peel, and put it in the trash. I'm thinking, great, this is over. Maybe she won't toss her banana debris into the bushes and we will have less flies. I'm sure I could have been more nice about it / sworn less, but I was just so shocked to see someone litter like that. I badged in to the building and she walked in behind me. At some point, she must have cried to her boss about it, because her boss found me today and asked if I confronted her intern. I said I had, then explained, as I have done here, about the banana peel. I guess she spent all morning crying about how "mean" I was and couldn't do any work. My brain was screaming "drama queen" but I apologized instead for upsetting the intern. We laughed together about absurdity of it all, especially over a banana peel! But now that it's the weekend and I'm sufficiently caffeinated, I'm wondering AITA for calling her out?

Diwali is next week and I still need to decorate the house and put up diyas before relatives arrive. What would you prioritize first?

Here’s a quick “Diwali‑to‑door” checklist that keeps the most important things front‑and‑center while still letting you finish the fun bits on time. | Priority | Why it matters | What to do (1‑2 hrs) | Quick Tips | |----------|----------------|----------------------|------------| | **1. Clean & declutter** | A tidy home feels festive and reduces fire risk. | • Sweep/ vacuum high‑traffic areas.
• Wipe down surfaces, especially kitchen counters and the living‑room.
• Put away clutter that could catch fire. | Use a “Diwali‑clean” playlist to keep the mood upbeat. | | **2. Safety check** | Diyas, candles, and decorations can be fire hazards. | • Inspect all electrical outlets and extension cords.
• Make sure no flammable material is near a light source.
• If you’re using real candles, keep them in sturdy holders and away from curtains. | Consider LED “diyas” or battery‑powered lanterns for a safer, longer‑lasting glow. | | **3. Diyas & lighting** | The glow is the heart of Diwali décor. | • Set up a central diyā‑rack or a string of LED diyas.
• Arrange a few “big” diyas on the main table or doorway.
• Add a few scented candles or incense sticks for aroma. | If you’re short on time, a pre‑lit LED diyā set can be plugged in and looks just as festive. | | **4. Decorative accents** | Adds color and atmosphere. | • Hang a few simple rangoli designs or paper lanterns.
• Place a small garland of marigold or artificial flowers.
• Add a few decorative pots or jars with fresh flowers. | Use items you already have—e.g., a string of fairy lights, a bowl of marigold petals, or a decorative bowl of sweets. | | **5. Food & sweets** | Guests will appreciate a warm welcome. | • Prep a quick snack platter (nuts, samosas, or a pre‑made sweet dish).
• Set up a small table with tea/coffee and a few plates. | If you’re short on time, order a ready‑made dessert or buy a pre‑packaged sweet box. | | **6. Final touches & personal flair** | Make it feel uniquely yours. | • Add a personal photo frame or a small family heirloom.
• Light a scented candle or a small incense stick.
• Put on a favorite playlist or a short devotional song. | Keep it simple—one or two personal touches can make a big difference. | ### A 3‑Day Mini‑Plan (if you have a week) | Day | Focus | Key Tasks | |-----|-------|-----------| | **Day 1** | Clean & safety | Deep clean, check outlets, set up a safe diyā area. | | **Day 2** | Diyas & décor | Install diyas, hang garlands, set up rangoli. | | **Day 3** | Food & final touches | Prep snacks, set the welcome table, add personal flair. | ### Quick “Do‑It‑Now” List (under 30 min) 1. **Sweep** the living room and kitchen floor. 2. **Plug in** a battery‑powered LED diyā set. 3. **Place** a few real candles in sturdy holders on the main table. 4. **Hang** a pre‑made paper lantern or a string of fairy lights. 5. **Set** a small plate of nuts or a pre‑made sweet on the welcome table. 6. **Light** a scented candle or incense stick. --- **Bottom line:** Start with cleaning and safety—those are the foundations. Once the house is safe and tidy, the diyas and décor will instantly lift the mood. Then finish with a quick food setup and a few personal touches. You’ll have a warm, welcoming home ready for your relatives in no time! Happy Diwali! 🌟
